candidates.attacker_control: The matched string is derived entirely from the attacker-controlled request line: request.getServletPath() and request.getPathInfo() (servlet-container-decoded path components, into which an encoded newline such as %0a is decoded). The attacker also controls the HTTP method considered at lines 86-89. No privileged position is required; a single unauthenticated request is enough.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked whether StrictHttpFirewall blocks the vector: it rejects only non-printable ASCII in the raw requestURI and blacklists semicolon, backslash, and encoded slash/dot/percent in encoded/decoded forms, but does not reject CR/LF in decoded servletPath/pathInfo (StrictHttpFirewall lines 290-333 and 368-399). Checked whether the URL is taken from the encoded requestURI instead of decoded values: lines 91-106 use getServletPath()/getPathInfo(), that is decoded values. Checked whether DOTALL is configured elsewhere: no compile flags beyond CASE_INSENSITIVE exist in this class. Checked that this is not dead code: AbstractRequestMatcherRegistry.regexMatchers and XML/web configuration paths instantiate this matcher, and DefaultFilterInvocationSecurityMetadataSource consumes it. Acknowledged limitation: exploitation additionally depends on the container decoding behavior and on the routing layer still dispatching the crafted path, which cannot be runtime-verified in this read-only review.
candidates.impact: Authorization bypass: a request to a protected URL can be evaluated against a less restrictive authorization rule, allowing unauthenticated or lower-privileged users to reach endpoints the configuration intended to restrict (for example administrative paths). This is a confidentiality/integrity impact on protected resources, not merely a hardening gap.
candidates.prerequisites: The application must use a RegexRequestMatcher (for example Java configuration regexMatchers("/admin/.*")... via AbstractRequestMatcherRegistry.regexMatchers, XML regex intercept-urls, or a directly constructed matcher) with a pattern containing a dot such as .*, and rely on rule ordering where a later rule is more permissive. The servlet container must pass the decoded newline through in servletPath/pathInfo, and the framework routing layer must still dispatch the crafted path to the protected handler. StrictHttpFirewall does not block this: its printable-ASCII check runs on the raw (still percent-encoded) requestURI, and its decoded-path blacklist (semicolon, percent, backslash, encoded slash, encoded dot) does not include CR/LF.
candidates.root_cause: RegexRequestMatcher builds its Pattern with Pattern.compile(pattern) (or Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE only) and then evaluates pattern.matcher(url).matches() against servletPath + pathInfo. Because Pattern.DOTALL is not set, the dot does not match line terminators. A URL whose decoded path contains a newline (for example a %0a encoded into the path) therefore fails to match a rule whose regex uses a dot (canonical example /admin/.*), even though the same request can still be dispatched by the application routing layer (Ant/PathPattern '**' matching tolerates the extra character in the last segment). The restricted authorization rule is skipped and the next matching rule (commonly anyRequest().permitAll() or a weaker rule) decides the request, producing an authorization bypass. The code is the pre-fix version of the upstream flaw later assigned CVE-2022-22978.
candidates.title: RegexRequestMatcher compiles patterns without DOTALL, allowing authorization-rule bypass via newline in the decoded request path
candidates.trace: 1) Config API creates the matcher: AbstractRequestMatcherRegistry.regexMatchers(...) leads to new RegexRequestMatcher(pattern, method) (config lines 290-298). 2) The RegexRequestMatcher constructor compiles the pattern without DOTALL (Pattern.compile(pattern) or Pattern.compile(pattern, Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE), lines 66-72). 3) matches() assembles url = servletPath + pathInfo (+ query string) from decoded request values (lines 91-106) and returns pattern.matcher(url).matches() (line 113). 4) With a newline in the decoded path, dot-based patterns that should describe the protected resource fail to match, and DefaultFilterInvocationSecurityMetadataSource returns the attributes of the next matching RequestMatcher instead. 5) The request proceeds with the weaker authorization decision while the application-level route (for example '**'-style handler mapping) still serves the protected endpoint, so the security rule is bypassed.
candidates.unverified: No runtime/container execution was performed. The precise set of containers that pass a decoded newline through to servletPath/pathInfo was not verified, and the exact application routing behavior needed to reach the protected handler is inferred from framework matching semantics rather than executed. Whether the benchmark's intended flaw is this same code path is unknown.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-436 Interpretation Conflict / CWE-863 Incorrect Authorization (authorization-rule bypass in URL matching)

coverage_summary: The source scope reports 1597 readable files (no symlinks, no sensitive-path exclusions, no files over 5 MiB skipped); only text/binary filtering applies, so this is the full visible tree. I covered all main modules at least at file/structure level (core, web, config, crypto, acl, ldap, cas, openid, messaging, oauth2-core/client/jose/resource-server, taglibs, remoting, data, aspects, samples) and read in depth the authorization pipeline (AbstractSecurityInterceptor, FilterSecurityInterceptor, AccessDecisionManagers/Voters, expression handling, URL matchers, security metadata sources), the authentication pipeline (AbstractUserDetailsAuthenticationProvider, DaoAuthenticationProvider, password encoders, remember-me, session strategies, anonymous/remember-me filters), CSRF/header/firewall handling, saved-request/redirect handling, OAuth2 login/authorization-code response validation, LDAP encoding/search, and ACL permission granting. No precomputed source-relation index was available (B0 condition), so coverage is search-and-read based rather than an exhaustive line-by-line review of all 1597 files.
limitations: No test sources, build outputs, git history or commit metadata are present in the snapshot, so the exact upstream commit and any downstream fix cannot be confirmed from the tree.

No code was executed and no containers, scanners, or exploit payloads were used; container-specific URL decoding/dispatch behavior underlying the candidate exploitability is inferred, not runtime-confirmed.

Large files were reviewed selectively (for example HttpSecurity, ServerHttpSecurity, BasicLookupStrategy, DefaultSavedRequest, LdapUserDetailsManager) rather than exhaustively, so an unexamined defect in those areas cannot be excluded.
The candidate count is capped at one per this review; several weaker leads were examined and are listed as rejected rather than as additional candidates.

rejected_leads.lead: Open redirect in DefaultRedirectStrategy / saved-request handling (DefaultRedirectStrategy.calculateRedirectUrl, SavedRequestAwareAuthenticationSuccessHandler, DefaultSavedRequest)
rejected_leads.reason: The code matches the long-standing upstream implementation (absolute URLs are returned as-is only when contextRelative=false; saved requests are reconstructed from server-side request state). No attacker-controlled cross-origin redirect primitive could be traced to a specific transformation or validation gap.

rejected_leads.lead: BCrypt strength handling allows log rounds up to 31 (BCrypt.MAX_LOG_ROUNDS = 31; BCryptPasswordEncoder accepts 4..31)
rejected_leads.reason: Corresponds to an upstream integer-overflow issue later fixed (rounds above 30), but it is only reachable through developer configuration (no attacker-controlled input), and its impact (too few effective hashing rounds or resource exhaustion) is a weakness rather than a traceable external vulnerability. Weaker than the selected candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: DelegatingPasswordEncoder.matches returns true when both rawPassword and encoded password are null
rejected_leads.reason: Looks surprising but is not reachable from DaoAuthenticationProvider (it throws BadCredentialsException before calling the encoder when credentials are null), and the behavior matches upstream. No exploit path with source evidence could be constructed.

rejected_leads.lead: Remember-me token weaknesses (TokenBasedRememberMeServices MD5 signature; PersistentTokenBasedRememberMeServices non-constant-time String.equals for the token value)
rejected_leads.reason: Design/hardening weaknesses in upstream code; the signature input includes server-side key/password material, token values are random, and no practical attacker-controlled bypass could be traced from the source.

rejected_leads.lead: Open redirect or request-cache poisoning via continue/target-url request parameters
rejected_leads.reason: The relevant handlers either validate configured URLs via UrlUtils.isValidRedirectUrl or require the application to explicitly enable a target URL parameter; no unconditional attacker-controlled redirect path was found.

rejected_leads.lead: Session fixation strategies, concurrent-session control, CSRF filter, anonymous/remember-me authentication, ACL permission granting, OAuth2/OIDC state and redirect-uri validation, LDAP filter encoding
rejected_leads.reason: Read and compared their security-relevant logic against expected semantics (state equality checks, session migration checks, permission/SID matching, filter encoding). No defect with concrete attacker-controlled security impact was found.

summary: Reviewed the Spring Security snapshot (1597 readable source files, version 5.2.0.BUILD-SNAPSHOT, Spring Framework 5.1.1, Gradle 4.10.1) as a defensive source review. I traced attacker-controlled request data through URL matching, authorization, session/CSRF, remember-me, OAuth2/OIDC, LDAP, ACL, CAS, OpenID and crypto paths. Most security-critical classes match expected upstream semantics (vote tallying, AuthenticationProvider credential checks, StrictHttpFirewall blacklists/normalization, CSRF token comparison, session-fixation strategies, ACL permission granting, LDAP filter encoding). One concrete, CVE-backed authorization-bypass flaw is present in the URL matcher used by the regexMatchers() authorization API: RegexRequestMatcher is compiled without Pattern.DOTALL, so patterns such as /admin/.* do not match decoded request paths containing a newline; a restricted rule can therefore be skipped and a later, more permissive rule can authorize a request that the application still routes. This is the single strongest source-evidenced candidate; other suspicious spots were examined and rejected (listed below).
